'''''Echinochloa crus-galli''''' is a species of wild grass originating from tropical Asia that was formerly classified as a [[panicum]] grass. It is commonly known as '''cockspur''', '''cockspur grass''', '''barnyard grass''', '''barnyard millet''', '''water grass''', '''cocksfoot grass''', '''cockshin grass'''.<ref name=GRIN>{{GRIN |access-date=1 August 2026}}</ref> It is sometimes referred to using the general term, ''barnyard grass'', which may refer to any species of the genus ''[[Echinochloa]]''. This plant can grow to {{cvt|1.5|m|ft|0}} in height and has long, flat leaves which are often purplish at the base. Most stems are upright, but some will spread out over the ground. Stems are flattened at the base. The seed heads are a distinctive feature, often purplish, with large millet-like seeds in crowded [[spikelet]]s.

Considered one of the world's worst weeds, it reduces [[crop yields]] and causes [[forage crops]] to fail by removing up to 80% of the available [[soil]] [[nitrogen]]. It acts as a host for several [[mosaic virus]] diseases.<ref name="fao">Heuzé V., Thiollet H., Tran G., Lebas F., 2017. Cockspur grass (Echinochloa crus-galli) forage. Feedipedia, a programme by INRA, CIRAD, AFZ and FAO. https://www.feedipedia.org/node/451 {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180310010358/https://www.feedipedia.org/node/451 |date=10 March 2018 }}</ref> Heavy infestations can interfere with mechanical harvesting.

Individual plants can produce up to 40,000 seeds per year. Water, birds, insects, machinery, and animal feet disperse it, but contaminated seed is probably the most common dispersal method.

Leaves flat, [[Glossary of botanical terms#glabrous|glabrous]], elongate, {{cvt|30|–|50|cm}} long, {{cvt|1|-|2|cm}} broad, [[scabrous]], slightly thickened at margin; [[ligule]]s absent; [[Leaf sheath|sheath]]s smooth, lower ones often reddish; [[panicle]] 8–30 cm long, green or purple, exerted, somewhat nodding, densely branched, the branches to 5 cm long, erect or ascending [[Sessility (botany)|sessile]];

Spikelets {{cvt|3|–|4|mm}} long, densely arranged on branches, ovoid, often long-[[Awn (botany)|awned]], pale green to dull purple, short-bristly along veins; [[racemes]] spreading, ascending or appressed, the lower somewhat distant, as much as {{cvt|10|cm}} long, sometimes branched; [[glume]]s and lower [[lemma (botany)|lemma]] minutely hairy on surface with longer more rigid hairs on veins; first glume about two-fifths as long as spikelet, deltoid, the second as long as the spikelet, short-awned; sterile lemma membranous, with a straight scabrous awn, {{cvt|2|–|4|cm}} long or awnless; fertile lemma ovate-elliptic, acute, pale yellow, lustrous, smooth, {{cvt|3|–|3.5|mm}} long. Fl. Aug.–Oct.; seed maturing Sept.–Oct., up to 40,000/plant. Var. ==Distribution and habitat==
Barnyard grass commonly occurs in Europe and throughout tropical Asia and Africa in fields and along roadsides, ditches, along railway lines, and in disturbed areas such as gravel pits and dumps. It also invades riverbanks and the shores of lakes and ponds. It occurs in all agricultural regions. This species is considered an [[invasive species]] in North America where it occurs throughout the continental United States. It is also found in southern Canada from British Columbia east to [[Newfoundland (island)|Newfoundland]].<ref>http://www.natureserve.org/explorer/servlet/NatureServe?searchName=Echinochloa+crusgalli{{Dead link|date=March 2022 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }} Map showing distribution</ref> It was first spotted in the [[Great Lakes]] region in 1843.<ref>{{cite web |title=List of invasive species in the Great Lakes Great Lakes United / Union Saint-Grands Lacs |url=http://www.glu.org/en/node/199 |access-date=7 February 2009 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090429205753/http://www.glu.org/en/node/199 |archive-date=29 April 2009 }}</ref>

==Ecology==
Ranging from ''boreal moist'' to ''wet through tropical'' and ''very dry to moist forest'' [[Holdridge life zones|life zone]]s. Adapted to nearly all types of wet places, this grass is often a common weed in [[paddy field]]s, roadsides, cultivated areas, and fallow fields. It grows on variety of wet sites such as ditches, low areas in fertile croplands and wet wastes, often growing in water. It succeeds in cool regions, but is better adapted to areas where average annual temperature is {{cvt|14|–|16|°C}}. It is not restricted by [[soil pH]].<ref name="fao" />

==Usage==
''E. crus-galli'' was [[crop domestication|domesticated]] in [[southern Hokkaido]] 4,500 years ago.<ref name="Purugganan-Fuller-2009" />

A warm-season grass used as cattle [[fodder]] and is sometimes cultivated for this purpose. It is also suited for [[silage]], but not for [[hay]]. It is fed green to animals and provides fodder throughout the year; hay made from this plant can be kept up to 6 years. This grass is also used for reclamation of [[soil salinity|saline]] and [[alkaline]] areas, especially in Egypt.

This grass is readily eaten by rabbits, deer, and waterfowl.<ref name="fao" />

The grain of some varieties is eaten by humans in times of scarcity and sometimes used for [[Adulterant|adulterating]] [[fennel]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.hort.purdue.edu/newcrop/duke_energy/Echinochloa_crusgalli.html |title=''Echinochloa crusgalli'' |access-date=24 September 2007 |archive-date=17 October 2007 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071017031356/http://www.hort.purdue.edu/newcrop/duke_energy/Echinochloa_crusgalli.html |url-status=live }}</ref> The young shoots are eaten as a vegetable.

In the [[Hisar district]] of the Indian state of [[Haryana]] the seeds of this grass are commonly eaten with cultivated rice grains to make [[rice pudding]] or [[kheer|khir]] on [[Hindu]] [[Religious_fasting#Hinduism|fast days]].

Barnyard grass was one of the five most cultivated crops during [[Joseon Dynasty]] in Korea.

[[Echinochloa esculenta|Japanese barnyard millet]] (''Echinochloa esculenta'' syn. ''E. cg.'' var. ''utilis''),<ref name="Purugganan-Fuller-2009" /> a domesticated form of ''E. crus-galli'', is cultivated on a small scale in Japan, Korea and China. It underwent [[plant breeding|selection]] for larger grain size over a span of one or two millennia in Japan.<ref name="Purugganan-Fuller-2009" />

==Diseases and pests==
This grass is subject to the brown spot disease caused by ''[[Bipolaris oryzae]]'', a [[fungal]] infection.
